subject: Simulating an AR(1) process: theta parameters of inla.spde2.precision

messages.author: 648de078c75a9b6b
messages.subject: Simulating an AR(1) process: theta parameters of inla.spde2.precision
parts:
Hi,

I am simulating a stationary AR(1) process of spatial fields in time (omega_(t+1) = phi * omega_t + epsilon_t) based on the theta1 and theta2 parameters of a random field generated with an INLA logistic model with a Matérn spatial component. To simulate random fields omega_(t+1) that maintain stationary variance similar to that of my original random field, I would need to simulate random fields (epsilon_t) using inla.spde2.precision and inla.qsample in which the variance compared to my original random field while keeping the spatial scale intact.

As I've understood that theta1 = log(tau) both the INLA Matérn model summary and in inla.spde2.precision and that tau^2 is in relation to sigma^2, the theta1 of the simulated epsilon_t fields should be set into theta1-log(1-phi^2). However, simulating the AR(1) process using these parameters does not lead into stationary variance, but the variance seems to increase with low values of phi and decrease with high values of phi.

How should I use the theta parameters of a Matérn model to scale the variance, but not the spatial scale, of simulated fields?
Many thanks!

Regards,
Henna Fabritius

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Simulating an AR(1) process: theta parameters of inla.spde2.precision
parts: As I've understood that theta1 = log(tau) both the INLA Matérn model summary and in inla.spde2.precision and that tau^2 is in relation to sigma^2,

They are related, yes, but they are not the same. For fields on R^2, the relationship is
sigma^2 = constant / kappa^2 / tau^2
the theta1 of the simulated epsilon_t fields should be set into theta1-log(1-phi^2).

Try
  theta1 + log(1-phi^2)
instead.

Also note that to get a constant variance over time you also need to make sure that the first field is simulated with the correct variance to match the stationary distribution of the process.

Finn
